Our commitment to marine biodiversity conservation is manifest in our continued focussed efforts to protect 
the Olive Ridley sea turtle along the Odisha coastline – one of the most significant nesting regions for the 
species globally.
Odisha’s coast is internationally recognised for hosting large nesting congregations of the Olive Ridley sea turtle 
– a vulnerable marine species distinguished by its rare mass-nesting behaviour which is marked by thousands 
of females gathering annually along their natal beaches. This natural phenomenon underscores the ecological 
importance of the region and the need for sustained conservation measures.
The coastal restoration work at Tuna – Kandla has taken a significant ecological leap by moving toward 
multi-species mangrove development. Traditionally, the region’s mangrove cover has been dominated by a 
single species, but this project is aimed at reintroducing species that were once a rare presence in Kachchh.
Tuna–Kandla Mangrove Bio‑shield: Reviving Multi‑ Species Diversity
 Conservation of Olive Ridley Sea Turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) in Odisha
Approach
 �Cultivation of a diverse mix of mangroves 
across the project area is gradually 
reshaping the ecology of the site
 �Early signs show these species adjusting 
well to the region’s challenging salinity 
levels, indicating strong potential for 
long-term establishment
Approach
 �Targeted actions have been undertaken to safeguard these sensitive marine species during critical nesting 
and migratory periods
 �Efforts are focussed on reducing human disturbances near nesting sites, supporting scientific research, 
facilitating safer near-shore movement and migration, and strengthening protection mechanisms across key 
nesting beachesImpact
 �Healthier, more layered mangrove structure – 
one that offers enhanced coastal protection, 
richer habitat value, and improved shoreline 
stability, is beginning to show along the coastline 
with the plantation maturing
 �Kachchh has taken a key step in transitioning 
from a largely uniform mangrove landscape to a 
more resilient, diverse ecosystem
Measures Taken
1. Protection of Nesting Habitats
 �Enhanced monitoring and patrolling 
undertaken across the nesting beaches to 
protect adult females and their nests during 
peak season
 �Patrolling support strengthened through the 
deployment of trawlers for surveillance and 
rescue operations
2. Dark Sky Lighting
 �Turtle-friendly, low glare lighting systems 
implemented near operational areas along the 
coast to minimise artificial light, which can 
disorient nesting females and hatchlings
3. Safe Navigation & Fishing Controls
 �Shipping lanes adjusted to avoid 
turtle congregation zones, reducing 
vessel-related disturbances
 �Fishing exclusion zones demarcated using 
buoys to prevent trawlers from entering 
sensitive areas during the nesting and 
hatching periods
 �Mandatory use of Turtle Excluder Devices 
(TEDs) in trawl fishing nets to significantly 
reduce incidental (bycatch) of non-target 
species
4.  Community Engagement for Turtle‑
Friendly Practices
 �Awareness campaigns conducted with 
local fishing communities to promote 
responsible fishing methods, reduce 
accidental bycatch, and build local 
stewardship for turtle conservation
5. Scientific Research
 �Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) 
signed by Dhamra Port, in collaboration 
with the Adani Foundation, with the 
Principal Chief Conservator of Forests 
(Wildlife), Government of Odisha, and the 
Wildlife Institute of India (WII), Dehradun, 
to undertake a scientific research study 
titled “Spatial Use, Near Shore Movements, 
and Migratory Behaviour of Olive Ridley 
Sea Turtles off the Odisha Coast”
 �Study planned for a three-year period 
(2025-2028), with funding for the first 
year disbursed by the Adani Foundation, 
and research activities for nesting season 
November 2025 – May 2026 being 
conducted by the research team of the 
Wildlife Institute of India

Biodiversity Park – Mundra
We have established a dedicated 
Biodiversity Park within the 
Nursery at Mundra for conserving 
indigenous plant species, 
enhancing habitat diversity, 
and strengthening long-term 
ecosystem resilience in the region.
The Biodiversity Park serves 
as a living repository of native 
flora, with over 58 indigenous 
Approach
 �Native trees, shrubs, grasses, climbers, 
and medicinal plants have been carefully 
selected to create micro-habitats that 
support local avifauna, pollinators, and 
small terrestrial species
 �Flowering and nectar-rich species 
have been incorporated to encourage 
the presence of bees, butterflies, and 
other beneficial insects, contributing 
to pollination services and improved 
ecological balanceplant species representing the 
natural vegetation of the Kutch 
landscape. The plantation design 
follows a layered, multi-tier 
vegetation structure, replicating 
natural forest ecosystems 
and supporting diverse 
ecological functions.
Designed as a low-input, 
climate-resilient landscape, the Biodiversity Park 
prioritises species adapted 
to local climatic conditions, 
thereby minimising irrigation 
requirements and reducing 
dependency on chemical 
inputs. This approach promotes 
sustainable horticulture 
practices while optimising 
resource efficiency.
Impact

 �Enhanced biodiversity, evidenced by increased 
bird activity, pollinator presence, and habitat 
utilisation by small fauna
 �Improved soil health through higher organic 
matter, microbial activity, and moisture retention
 �Contribution to natural carbon sequestration 
through increased tree and shrub biomass
 �Strengthened ecosystem resilience against 
salinity, heat stress, and drought, characteristic 
of the region
Colombo West International 
Terminal (Private) Limited

and coral reef rehabilitation 
undertaken by the Pro Green 
Laboratory of the University of 
Moratuwa. The initiative focusses 
on the restoration of a degraded 
(dead) coral reef ecosystem in 
Beruwala, adopting a science-based 
and ecosystem-led approach.
The programme involves reef 
cleaning, coral transplantation, and continuous research-based 
monitoring to restore coral cover, 
enhance marine biodiversity, and 
improve ecosystem functionality. 
Scientific monitoring forms a 
core component of the initiative, 
enabling the assessment of coral 
survival rates, reef health, and 
long-term ecological outcomes.
A key milestone under this initiative 
was achieved with the successful 
completion of the first coral 
replanting session on January 24, 
2026, marking the commencement 
of active restoration efforts at the site. The project is expected to 
contribute to the recovery of 
marine biodiversity, strengthen 
coastal ecosystem resilience, 
and generate valuable research 
insights to inform future reef 
restoration initiatives.
Through this partnership, CWIT 
aims to support nature-based 
solutions, advance marine 
conservation science, and 
contribute to long-term positive 
outcomes for coastal ecosystems 
and communities.Hazardous Oil Spill Prevention and Management
Our meticulously crafted Oil Spill Action Plan seeks to prevent and swiftly mitigate environment-endangering spills 
of hazardous substance. The plan is designed to ensure compliance with global best practices in spill management, 
by aligning with both the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (NOS-DCP) and standards set by the 
International Petroleum Industry Environmental Conservation Association.
Performance Metrics: 0 L/crore (Volume of oil spilled/revenue)1.  Utilisation of leak-proof containers for transporting 
waste materials
2.  Secure storage of hazardous waste in closed 
containers
3.  Proper stacking and management of containers to 
prevent accidental spills
4.  Use of tarpaulins to cover waste-loaded transport 
vehicles, ensuring containment
5.  Provision of first-aid kits for immediate response to 
minor injuries that may occur during handling
6.  Conducting periodic inspections to proactively 
identify and rectify potential spill risks
7.  Implementing safe working procedures and training 
for personnel involved in handling and operational 
activitiesKey Aspects of Oil Spill Action Plan
 �Extensive Coverage: The plan addresses 
potential spill scenarios during 
anchoring, berthing, and cargo handling, 
encompassing a wide range of operational 
activities that could cause spills.
 �Regular Maintenance and Inspection: 
A regime of scheduled inspections and 
maintenance is integral to the plan, 
focussing on preventive measures to 
minimise the risk of spills. This includes 
ensuring the integrity and proper 
functioning of equipment and containment 
systems.
 �Effective Land Spill Management: 
Recognising that spills can also occur 
on land with detrimental effects on soil, 
habitats and terrestrial life, the plan 
includes specific strategies for immediate 
spill control and cleanup onshore.
 �Zero Spills Achievement: In the fiscal year 
2025-26, APSEZ successfully achieved zero 
spills, highlighting the effectiveness of its 
spill prevention and response strategies.The 7‑Point Oil Spill Action Plan

Enabling a Just and Inclusive Workforce Transition
Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd. integrates Just Transition principles into its long-term 
ESG and sustainable growth strategy to ensure that business transformation driven by automation, 
digitalisation, decarbonisation and acquisitions, remains responsible and people-centric. As the 
organisation’s scales its ports and logistics infrastructure, workforce transition is managed through 
a structured and inclusive approach focussing on long-term and shared value creation. We have 
implemented several measures to reduce social transition risks while reinforcing the organisation’s 
commitment to responsible employment practices.

At the Adani Group, learning is positioned as a strategic 
enabler of organisational excellence, leadership readiness 
and future-critical skill building. Our learning ecosystem 
is designed to strengthen execution capability, prepare 
employees for evolving business challenges and build a 
resilient workforce capable of sustaining long-term growth.  
Learning interventions are intentionally aligned with the 
organisation’s growth charter, operational priorities, and 
future skill requirements. These interventions enable future 
skill pathways by building skills in digital enablement, 
responsible business practices, climate and sustainability 
imperatives, and data-driven decision-making, embedded 
across roles and leadership levels. These programmes are 
delivered through a blended learning ecosystem and are 
applicable to permanent, contractual and, where relevant, 
other than permanent employees. Employee development 
programmes, including technical training, digital 
upskilling, safety, and behavioural training, are extended 
to contractual and site-based workforce, where relevant 
to role and operational requirements. This forward-looking 
approach to capability development directly contributes to 
business outcomes rather than remaining activity-driven.

Performance‑Linked 
Compensation
Based on the employee grades, a 
significant portion of the Total Cost 
to Company (CTC) is allocated as 
performance-based incentives:
 �O1 to E1 Grades: 10% of the CTC 
is linked to Performance-based 
incentive
 �E2 to E4 Grades: 15% of the CTC 
is linked to Performance-based 
incentive
 �General Manager (GM) and 
Above:  Performance pay is 
linked to a combination of 
individual performance and 
organisational outcomes, 
including Environmental, Social, 
and Governance (ESG) objectives
Performance pay is determined 
through organisation’s four-point 
scale within the Performance 
Management System, with 
qualitative adjustments made 
for ESG performance and safety 
considerations in the case of senior 
management personnel.
Performance Pay Components
 �Individual Performance (70%): 
Covers individual goal and ESG 
performance
 �Organisation Performance (30%): 
Measured in terms of business 
goals and financial performance, 
with a weightage of 50% on 
revenue, 25% on EBITDA, and 25% 
on Return on Capital Employed 
(RoCE)ESG‑Linked Performance
APSEZ has strategically integrated 
Environment, Social and Governance 
(ESG) performance into executive 
compensation, aligning individual 
contributions with organisations 
ESG imperatives. The evaluation 
metrics include compliance with the 
Code of Conduct, Human Rights, 
Financial and Operational Targets, 
Risk Management, IT, Cybersecurity, 
and Customer Satisfaction.
CEO’s Compensation Structure
CEO’s remuneration comprises fixed 
salary, variable pay, and long-term 
incentive. The variable pay and 
long-term incentive are linked to 
both financial and ESG indicators, 
including Total Shareholder Return, 
Revenue, EBITDA, ROCE, Health 
& Safety Metrics, Human Rights 
Parameters, Energy Intensity, 
GHG Intensity, Water Intensity, 
Zero Waste to Landfill (ZWL), 
and Mangrove Afforestation 
(Biodiversity).
Remuneration of the Executive 
Directors, and the CEO is 
recommended by the Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee 
(NRC), based on industry 
benchmarks, the company’s 
performance vis-à-vis the industry, 
Tobin’s Q, individual responsibilities, 
and performance/track record.
Succession Planning
APSEZ maintains a structured 
succession planning framework for 
critical leadership and strategic roles that applies to all employees 
in the 01 level and higher, including 
the CEOs. The framework is 
supported by a robust responsibility 
matrix that identifies, develops 
company’s future leaders, and 
specifies roles and responsibilities 
of the senior management and the 
human resources department.
Critical roles are systematically 
identified through an evaluation 
led by the HR Head (Operating Unit 
/ Corporate) and the COO / the 
CEO / Business Head. Positions are 
categorised based on:
 �Organisation’s ability to sustain its 
business operations and avoid any 
adverse effect it might face as a 
result of such vacancy
 �Ease of availability and quality of 
such resource / skills in the talent 
market
 �Contribution to the topline / 
bottom-line in terms of Gross 
Revenue, Net Profit and EBIDTA, 
in absolute relative terms
The process also considers the 
organisation’s five-year business 
strategy to ensure leadership 
readiness for future priorities. 
Positions are categorised 
accordingly and succession 
plans are reviewed annually, 
or earlier in case of significant 
business changes. This structured 
approach ensures transparency, 
leadership pipeline strength and 
alignment with APSEZ’s long-term 
growth objectives.Diversity Equity and Inclusion

Care and Motivation
Employee Wellbeing and Support
The Adani Group recognises that holistic wellbeing is vital to building a resilient, engaged and high-performing 
workforce. Our approach goes beyond traditional workplace benefits to create a holistic ecosystem that supports 
employees across their professional and personal lives. Through a multi-dimensional framework, we address the 
physical, mental, emotional and financial wellbeing of our people. This framework is supported by initiatives that 
promote work-life balance, safety, quality of life and family welfare for both office-based and site-based employees.Adani Group places strong 
emphasis on psychological 
safety, enabling employees to 
express views, raise concerns 
and share ideas without fear 
of retaliation.
Wellbeing of Remote and Site‑
Based Workforce
Safety and wellbeing of our 
workers operating in geographically 
isolated and high risk environments 
is treated as core operational 
priorities, not peripheral HR 
initiatives. The organisation 
integrates mental wellbeing into 
Occupational Health & Safety 
Management Systems (OHSMS). 
By integrating safety systems, 
accessible healthcare and worker 
welfare infrastructure, the 
organisation ensures physical safety, mental resilience and 
dignified living conditions for 
site-based workers.
Safety‑First Wellbeing Culture
 �Regular safety campaigns, drills 
and tool-safety inspections
 �Leadership-led safety engagement 
at sites

Respecting and 
protecting people rights
At APSEZ, we consider human rights to be the fundamental, universal and inalienable 
entitlements that every person holds simply by virtue of being human. We strongly believe 
that these rights are universally applicable to all, regardless of race, sex, nationality, 
ethnicity, language, religion, or any other status. Such rights span a wide range – extending 
from the most basic, such as the right to life and liberty, and freedom from slavery and 
torture, to essential civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights, including freedom of 
opinion and expression, the right to work, education, health, and more.
As a people forward organisation, APSEZ recognises the potential of its business to impact 
human rights across the value chain. We are resolutely committed to respecting and 
supporting all human rights in our operations, value chain, and services, in accordance with 
international standards and applicable law. Our approach to the protection of human rights 
is aligned to the overall Adani Group philosophy. It is driven by our proactive policies and 
actions aimed at safeguarding the interests of the people in our stakeholder universe.SDG Alignment

Human Rights Policy 
Effectiveness Monitoring 
Framework 
Our human rights strategy involves 
continuous and effective monitoring 
of our policy, with a well-defined 
process in place to track and assess 
its implementation. The step-by-
step strategy involves:
1. Data Collection & Insights: 
Gathering information from diverse 
sources, including grievance 
mechanisms, employee engagement 
surveys, internal audits, and supplier 
assessments, to identify potential 
risks and trends.
2. Performance Measurement: 
Tracking key human rights 
indicators, such as: percentage of 
workforce trained on human rights 
and DEI principles, number and 
nature of complaints related to 
human rights violations, frequency 
and scope of human rights impact 
assessments across operations 
and supply chains.
3. Independent Review & 
Fact‑Finding: Conduct of 
thorough investigations by our 
Risk Management Committee 
into reported issues, ensuring 
impartiality and accountability 
in addressing concerns related 
to human rights.
4. Preventive & Corrective Actions: 
Implementation of proactive 
measures to prevent violations, 
and take swift, appropriate 
corrective actions whenever 
non-compliance is detected.
5. Continuous Improvement 
& Transparency: Conduct of 
regular reviews, enabling course 
correction and policy enhancement, 
followed by transparent 
communication of findings 
and progress to stakeholders Heightened Due Diligence

Salient Human Rights Risks
Driven by our non-negotiable respect for human rights, we have prioritised the following human rights issues to be 
addressed across our businesses and value chains.
Child Labour Fair Wages Equal Remuneration
Working Hours Health & Safety Harassment Discrimination
Forced LabourFair Wages and Pay Equity
Definitions
1. Forced Labour: Forced labour 
refers to any work or service that 
is exacted from an individual under 
the threat of penalty, and for which 
the individual has not offered 
voluntary service. Indicators of 
forced labour include, but are not 
limited to, unreasonable recruitment 
fees leading to debt bondage, 
deception, restriction of movement, 
isolation, abuse of vulnerability, 
intimidation or threats, abusive 
living or working conditions, 
withholding of wages, excessive 
overtime, and retention of personal 
identity documents.
2. Child Labour: Child labour 
constitutes work that deprives 
children of their childhood, 
dignity, and potential, and is 
harmful to their physical or mental 
development. It includes work that 
is mentally, physically, socially, or 
morally harmful to children, and 
interferes with their education 
by preventing school attendance, 
causing premature school dropouts, 
or requiring them to combine 
schooling with excessively 
long or heavy work.Risk Exposure across the Value 
Chain
Risks related to forced labour 
and child labour may arise across 
communities and supply chains, 
particularly in warehousing 
operations, transportation, 
construction activities, and 
upstream material sourcing. 
Groups most vulnerable to 
such risks include migrant 
workers, agency and third-party 
workers, temporary and 
self-employed workers, as well as 
women and children.
Risk Prevention 
At APSEZ, we work closely with 
suppliers and business partners to 
strengthen ethical labour practices 
and responsible recruitment 
systems across the value chain. 
We have launched various human 
rights risk prevention measures to 
strengthen our people risk redressal 
system. These include:
 �A Responsible Recruitment 
Policy clearly articulating the 
supplier’s responsible recruitment 
commitment, setting expectations 
internally and externally for agencies, sub-contractors, 
and importantly, their other 
suppliers (our tier two 
suppliers)
 �Clear contracts with 
agencies covering clauses 
relating to prohibition of 
passport retention, payment 
of recruitment fees, and 
prohibition of child labour
 �Training for management 
and workers to understand 
the key components of 
responsible recruitment and 
its importance, and providing 
transparency for workers on 
their rights
 �Grievance mechanisms 
allowing workers the 
opportunity to confidently 
raise any concerns they 
may have
 �Background verification for 
each of the employees and 
workers
 �Mandatory checks of 
government issued ID proofs Definitions
1. Fair Wages: This refers to 
remuneration that meets or 
exceeds statutory minimum wage 
requirements, and is sufficient to 
cover the basic needs of workers 
and their families, while also 
providing a reasonable level of 
discretionary income.
2. Equal Remuneration: This 
is based on the principle that 
women and men should receive 
equal pay for work of equal value. 
This principle applies not only to 
identical or similar roles but also 
to different roles that are assessed 
as being of equal value, based on 
objective criteria such as skills, 
qualifications, working conditions, 
levels of responsibility, and 
effort required.Risk Exposure across the Value 
Chain
Risks related to unfair wages and 
unequal remuneration may arise 
primarily within supply chains, 
particularly in labour-intensive 
and low-skilled segments. 
Vulnerable groups include workers 
engaged in part-time employment, 
outsourced activities, and 
contract-based arrangements.
Risk Prevention
 �Prior to onboarding, suppliers 
are required to demonstrate 
compliance with all applicable 
labour laws and regulations, 
including statutory minimum 
wage requirements �The Company’s remuneration 
practices comply with 
applicable laws in all 
jurisdictions where it 
operates. For Indian entities, 
this includes adherence to 
the Government of India’s 
Code on Wages, 2019, while 
international entities follow 
the respective local labour 
and wage regulations of their 
countries
 �Periodic reviews of wage 
and salary structures are 
conducted to identify and 
address potential disparities, 
and ensure alignment with 
legal, ethical, and internal 
policy requirements

Prevention of Discrimination & Harassment
Definitions
1. Discrimination: It refers to any 
unfair, unequal, or humiliating 
treatment of individuals on the 
basis of gender, sexual orientation, 
race, colour, age, pregnancy, marital 
or social status, religion, political 
opinion, nationality, ethnic origin, 
disease, disability, or any other 
legally protected characteristic.
2. Harassment: It relates to violence 
and harassment directed at persons 
because of their sex or gender, or 
affecting persons of a particular sex 
or gender disproportionately and 
includes sexual harassment.
Risk Exposure Across the 
Value Chain
Risks related to discrimination 
and harassment may arise within 
the company’s own operations 
or at any point across its value 
chain. They are particularly likely 
to arise where unconscious bias, 
entrenched workplace behaviours, or discriminatory practices exist. 
Vulnerable groups may include 
women, local communities, migrant 
workers, LGBTQIA+ individuals, and 
minority groups.
Risk Prevention
 �We are firmly committed to 
upholding the rights of all 
employees and associates 
to express themselves freely 
in a workplace, devoid of 
discrimination or harassment, 
including sexual and non-sexual 
harassment and exploitation. 
We continually invest in fostering 
a safe and inclusive work 
culture, and have implemented 
a zero-tolerance policy aligned 
with the Sexual Harassment of 
Women at Workplace (Prevention, 
Prohibition, and Redressal) Act, 
2013, applicable to all employees. 
Corrective or disciplinary action is 
taken in cases of discriminatory 
behaviour or harassment �Suppliers are audited for their 
policy commitment as well as 
their systems and processes, in 
order to ensure prevention of 
harassment and discrimination
 �Employees experiencing

The Adani Safety Management System comprises:Structured OHS Governance Framework
At APSEZ, we have put in place an exhaustive and structured Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) governance 
framework, encompassing all our manufacturing locations and the entire workforce. We are continually striving to

Key Enablers of our OHS Management System 
We have adopted a rigorous and structured approach to OHS management, aimed at proactively identifying hazards, 
mitigating risks, and promoting a culture of safety across all our operations.
Elaborate Internal

Regular Internal  
Safety Audits
Regular and comprehensive internal inspections and audits are carried 
out to systematically assess operational risks, potential hazards, and 
compliance gaps. These evaluations form the backbone of our risk 
management framework, and ensure that all safety critical aspects of 
operations receive continuous oversight.
All identified risks are prioritised based on severity, likelihood, and 
potential impact. These risks are then integrated into detailed action 
plans with clearly-defined targets and timelines. This structured 
approach ensures that health and safety concerns are addressed in a 
strategic and timely manner, reducing the probability of recurrence.
OHS site heads undertake continual monitoring of the progress 
against the established targets. Regular review of corrective and 
preventive actions helps ensure accountability, and allows for prompt 
intervention wherever gaps or delays are observed.
In the event of an incident or occurrence of an identified risk, a uniform 
investigation procedure – aligned with our OHS management system 
– is promptly activated. The procedure involves root cause analysis, 
documentation, corrective action planning, and knowledge dissemination, 
thereby reinforcing the preventive safety culture across sites.
To uphold the highest safety standards and ensure compliance with 
statutory requirements, periodic internal safety audits are conducted 
in accordance with the Factories Act. These audits help validate the 
effectiveness of our safety systems, highlight improvement areas, and 
strengthen organisational readiness.Securing the Workplace 
with OHS Policy

Strategic Dimensions for Enhancing Safety at APSEZ: The 5C Model
With safety embedded in our operations as a core value, it is our continuous endeavour to strengthen the 
safety culture and performance across the organisation. The 5C Model is an elaborate strategic framework to 
propel our safety enhancement efforts. The model is pillared around five key elements of the safety strategy, 
namely Commitment, Capability, Conformance, Communication, and Culture.
Elements of the 5C Model 
This model strategically blends theoretical understanding with practical applications, and improves 
the safety environment through comprehensive discussions, case studies, and interactive exercises. 
It ensures sustained compliance, minimisation of incidents, and promotion of a culture of continual 
learning with respect to safety. 
At APSEZ, we are committed to aligning our OHS structure with 
internationally benchmarked safety standards by following a 
process of continual engagement and assessment.Establishment of clear safety objectives and resource allocation 
by the leadership, which leads by example, ensures that safety 
remains the top priority in all organisational decisions. Continuous 
improvement is driven by regular audits and assessments.
Commitment
Training programmes, underlined by interactive modules and real-
life scenarios, boost learning by equipping employees with essential 
safety skills and knowledge.
Capability
Compliance is ensured through well-structured safety policies and 
procedures mapped to the highest industry standards. Corrective 
actions are taken in case of compliance failure.
Conformance
Safety information is disseminated through a variety of channels, 
including meetings, newsletters and digital platforms. Employees 
are encouraged through direct and open communication to report 
hazards and near-misses.
Communication
Safety is integrated into the organisation’s culture as a shared 
value and collective responsibility, and is nurtured  through 
ownership and accountability. Safe behaviour is rewarded through 
recognition programmes.

Impactful Initiatives to Boost Safety and Productivity
Our Contractor Incubation Series is structured to promote experience-based learnings. The initiatives under this 
series are mainly targeted at owners, managers, supervisors, and workers.
This key initiative is focussed on promoting safety skills among the workers of the contractors 
involved in the execution of most of our projects. Saksham is deployed by site heads, line managers 
and training coordinators. A Trainer's Handbook is also made available to ensure uniform training 
and live demonstrations. All contractors are onboarded on to Saksham before the start of any job 
and non-compliance is taken seriously, leading to disciplinary action as per Adani's Consequence 
Management Policy.
Saksham involves nurturing “Experience-based Learnings” through 3D animated modules, powered by 
trainers. It further entails training of coordinators and the OH&S team in the maintenance of records 
and feedback forms, which are evaluated by the Business Units (BUs) to strengthen the training process.
Both Saksham and the Trainer’s Handbook kits can easily be accessed and downloaded from the Group 
Safety Portal and Safety e-LMS Platform.
We have deployed Samwaad as a platform to drive enhanced participation, engagement and knowledge 
sharing by workers with respect to health and safety. It involves the use of the 'Adani SafeX' system, 
which facilitates employees in reporting any safety concerns or incidents within 40 seconds via their 
smartphones. This enables prompt handling of the concern/incident. Anonymous reporting is provided 
as an option in this system.SAKSHAM

process safety at APSEZ.

Oil Spill Contingency Plan
We have in place a comprehensive Oil Spill Contingency Plan to handle Tier 1 responses for up to 700 tonnes of 
oil, deemed to be the worst-case scenario. The plan is aligned with the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency 
Plan (NOS-DCP). It involves quick mobilisation of essential equipment and trained personnel to tackle any oil spill 
emergency. The plan ensures our preparedness to efficiently handle oil spill emergencies, thus protecting our 
operations and the environment.

Sensor Installation at Adani Gangavaram Port Ltd. (AGPL)
Safety and efficiency has been strengthened at Adani Gangavaram Port Ltd. (AGPL) with the installation of 
SUL-2, SUL-3 and SUL-4 sensors on gantry cranes and spill plates. Besides detecting obstacles and creating 
safety zones, the sensors automatically stop or slow down machinery in the event of detection of an 
object. This reduces the risk of accidents, preventing collisions in vessel operations, while also minimising 
damage and repair costs.  The reduction in downtime helps improve operational efficiency, enabling cranes 
to operate at optimal speeds. Real-time data and alerts help in better equipment management.

and co‑create solutions that deliver long‑term value. In collaboration with the Adani

About The Adani Foundation‑
Seva Since 1996 
We implement our CSR initiatives 
through the Adani Foundation, the 
social welfare and development arm 
of the Adani Group, established in 
1996. For nearly three decades, the 
Foundation has served as a catalyst 
for inclusive and sustainable 
development, translating the Adani 
Group’s purpose and philosophy 
into meaningful, on-ground action 
across India. It continues to walk 
alongside communities- listening, 
learning, and partnering to create 
pathways for opportunity, resilience, 
and shared progress. 
The Foundation works across 
geographies with a life-cycle 
approach and inclusive framework 
to enable change where it 
matters the most. Currently, it is 
operating in 7,247 villages across 
22 states, positively impacting 
13.3 million lives. Its interventions 
span critical development areas, 
including education, health and 
nutrition, sustainable livelihoods, 
climate action, and community 
development, with a strong 
focus on children, women, youth, 
and marginalised populations. 
The strategies of the Foundation 
are aligned with national priorities 
and Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs), ensuring that its initiatives 
contribute to nation-building and 
holistic development.Strategic Approach to 
Promoting Self‑Reliance and 
Lasting Empowerment 
Adani Foundation’s CSR approach is 
closely aligned with the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs), 
addressing national priorities such 
as poverty reduction, livelihoods. 
Its bottom-up, community-driven 
model operates through Village level 
institutions, ensuring participation 
from local leaders, civil society, 
experts, and marginalised groups, 
and is supported by an integrated 
grievance redressal system.
The Foundation prioritises 
inclusiveness, focussing on 
vulnerable communities including 
fisherfolk, tribal groups, children 
and women. Flagship initiatives 
like SuPoshan enhance women’s 
nutrition, social status, and 
incomes through dairy livelihood 
cooperatives and self-help groups. Environmental sustainability is 
ensured through green cover 
restoration, water conservation 
projects such as pond deepening 
and rainwater harvesting, and 
localised groundwater mitigation.
Biodiversity conservation is another 
focus area, with initiatives designed 
around the protection of coastal 
and terrestrial ecosystems across 
industrial sites. The Foundation 
also demonstrated empathy during 
crises, such as floods, cyclones, 
and the COVID-19 pandemic, 
through relief efforts and volunteer 
engagement. Collaboration with 
government bodies and civil 
society organisations strengthens 
programmes such as Utthan 
and Swabhiman. Across all 
initiatives, our priority remains on 
generating meaningful impact and 
enhancing the overall well-being 
of communities.Target Communities
The target communities consist 
of populations living in areas 
around Adani Port & Special 
Economic Zone (APSEZ) facilities. 
Project areas across several 
locations – Mundra, Dahej, Hazira, 
Dhamra, Dighi, Gopalpur, Kattupalli, 
Krishnapattanam, Karaikal, 
Gangavaram, Vizhinjam. The primary 
target groups are school going 
children, livestock-dependent 
households, women, farmers, 
cattle owners, and youth who 
face persistent challenges such as 
lack of quality education facility, 
limited livelihood opportunities, and 
restricted access to healthcare and 
basic infrastructure.
Strategy to Strengthen 
Community Relationships and 
Social License to Operate
The entity follows a participatory, 
community-centric model in 
villages around port businesses, 
building trust through regular 
village consultations, need 
assessments, and partnerships 
with local self-governance 
bodies, district administration, 
and community organizations. 
A consistent on-ground presence, 
transparent communication, and 
grievance mechanisms strengthen 
inclusion and accountability. 
Development initiatives to 
strengthen the state of primary 
education, public health, water 
security, and livelihoods are 
designed around local priorities, 
ensuring community ownership 
and reinforcing the entity’s role 
as a long-term development 
partner while striving to enhance 
transparency, build mutual trust, 
and strengthen community connect.

Community Risk 
Management
Key community risks in areas of 
operation of Adani Port and Special 
Economic Zone include degrading quality of education, water 
scarcity, climate-driven livelihood 
vulnerability, low levels of skills 
among youth, and environmental 
concerns. These risks are integrated 
into the Enterprise Risk Assessment 
Process through regular social risk 
assessments, stakeholder feedback, 
and site-level risk registers and are 
categorized by severity, likelihood, 
and their impact on community 
and business operations for a 
comprehensive oversight.
Mitigation Approach, 
Monitoring and Review 
Mechanism
All these risks exacerbate the 
vulnerability of the local population 
which APSEZ’s initiatives seek 
to address through targeted 
interventions in Education, Health 
& Nutrition, Livelihoods, Climate 
Action, and basic Infrastructure 
Development. Healthcare and 
nutrition challenges are addressed 
through intervention woven 
around provisioning doorstep 
primary healthcare services. 
Livelihood vulnerabilities 
are mitigated by promoting 
income diversification, skill development, and enterprise 
support. Environmental risks 
are managed through green 
belt development, continuous 
monitoring, and compliance 
with statutory norms. Water and 
climate risks are mitigated through 
rainwater harvesting, augmenting 
water conservation capacity, and 
promoting efficient water-use 
practices. All interventions are 
monitored through defined 
indicators, field reviews, beneficiary 
feedback, audits, impact 
assessments, and third-party 
evaluations, ensuring adaptive and 
responsive management.
Investments in Risk 
Management and Mitigation
Sustained investments are made in 
education, healthcare infrastructure 
and access to primary healthcare, 
water security, livelihood 
diversification & skill enhancement, 
environmental safeguards, and 
community capacity-building 
initiatives to enhance community 
resilience and ensure long-term 
risk mitigation.

Accountability 
Our CSR policy forms the

Community Grievance 
Mechanism:
APSEZ maintains a formally 
structured and transparent 
community grievance management 
process as part of its broader 
stakeholder-engagement and 
CSR framework. All community 
submissions are systematically 
logged, categorised, reviewed, 
and escalated through defined 
governance channels, with 
time-bound resolution protocols 
to ensure accountability and 
responsiveness. This structured 
approach strengthens trust, 
reinforces predictability, 
and ensures consistent 
closure of grievances in line 
with our commitment to 
stakeholder well-being.To further elevate transparency 
and organisation-wide consistency, 
APSEZ is implementing an 
Integrated Grievance Management 
System (IGMS). The system will 
enable community members and 
other stakeholders to digitally 
submit grievances, track the 
real-time status of their cases, 
monitor turnaround timelines, and 
provide feedback post-resolution. 
Once fully deployed, the IGMS 
will serve as a unified platform 
for centralised monitoring, 
analytics-based insights, and 
continuous improvement.

Implementation Methods for 
CSR Projects:
Projects are executed directly 
by the company or through 
its foundations and agencies, 
with collaboration permitted 
among companies.
 �Direct Method: Company or its 
foundation implements projects
 �Indirect Method: Through 
agencies with a track record of 
at least three years, monitored 
quarterly
 �Collaboration among Group 
Companies is allowed for project 
execution
Monitoring and Review 
Mechanism:
A review committee comprising site 
heads, employees, and Foundation 
representatives meets quarterly to 
monitor progress �Reports are submitted to the

 �Regular audits, capacity building, 
and performance reviews are 
conducted
Fund Allocation and Financial 
Guidelines
The company aims to spend at 
least 2% of the average net profits 
of the previous three years on CSR 
annually, with no statutory cap.
 �The CSR Annual Plan includes 
project details, expenditure, and 
schedules, approved by the Board
 �Surplus funds from CSR projects 
do not form part of business 
profits
 �Up to 5% of the approved budget 
can be used for capacity buildingResponsibilities of the Board 
and CSR Committee
The Board reports on CSR activities 
in its annual report, while the 
CSR Committee monitors policy 
implementation, reviews projects, 
and ensures transparency.
 �The Committee meets at least 
twice a year
 �The CSR policy and annual plan 
are displayed on the company's 
website
Review and Amendments
The CSR policy is reviewed every 
two years or earlier if needed, with 
the CSR Committee empowered 
to revise or amend the policy 
periodically. Ensures the policy 
remains aligned with statutory 
updates and organizational goals.Participatory Approach for 
CSR Implementation
Our CSR implementation 
follows a participatory 
approach, driven by continuous 
engagement with communities 
and stakeholders across our 
operations. We proactively 
identify and engage peripheral 
communities to foster meaningful 
dialogue and participation. 
Structured engagement and 
consultation processes enable 
communities to share their 
perspectives on operational 
and project-related risks, environmental and social impacts, 
and potential mitigation measures. 
These insights are systematically 
integrated into project planning 
and decision-making, ensuring 
alignment with evolving 
community needs. 
Robust grievance redressal 
and reporting mechanisms are 
in place to address concerns 
promptly, strengthening trust 
and transparency throughout 
the process. By prioritising 
listening, partnership, and shared 
decision-making, we deliver 
meaningful project outcomes that support sustainable development 
of communities.
The target communities in the areas 
of operation are identified through 
a combination of socio-economic 
profiling, geographic 
vulnerability assessment, and an 
understanding of local livelihood 
patterns. The target groups are 
selected based on:
Rural and socio‑economic 
vulnerability: Households with 
limited income sources and reliance 
on climate-sensitive livelihoods.
Livelihood dependency: 
Small and marginal farmers, 
pastoral communities, and 
families dependent on 
traditional occupations.
Social inclusivity needs: Women-led 
households, youth, and persons 
with disabilities requiring enhanced 
access to opportunities.
Geographic proximity to 
development corridors: 
Economically vulnerable households 
living in villages near plant and large 
infrastructure project sites, where 
rapid development increases the 
need for community support.
Agrarian and pastoral livelihoods: 
Households dependent on 
farming, livestock, and related 
rural occupations.
Socially and geographically 
marginalized groups: Villages 
located in remote area locations 
with poor access to basic services.
Economic vulnerability: Women, 
youth, artisans, and small 
traders with limited income 
diversification opportunities.
Cultural and traditional 
occupations: Groups engaged 
in crafts and trade, requiring 
support for skill development 
and market access.

Major CSR Interventions 
Education
The Adani Foundation believes 
that education is a powerful 
catalyst for social and economic 
transformation, especially in 
rural and underprivileged areas. 
Recognising this, the Foundation 
champions education not only 
as a fundamental right but as a 
transformative force that fuels 
aspirations and opportunities. We 
remain committed to empowering 
children with knowledge, critical 
thinking and confidence to build 
better futures.
Through an extensive network of 43 
schools, strategic partnerships, and 
pioneering programmes, the Adani 
Foundation aims to make quality 
learning accessible, aspirational, and 
inclusive for all. With its flagship 
initiatives, such as Project Utthan, 
which focusses on improving learning 
and academic outcomes, and Udaan, 
which encourages students to dream 
big and explore possibilities, the 
Foundation is effectively shaping the 
aspirations of young India, nurturing 
the next generation of leaders and 
innovators and building a more 
equitable future. Adani Vidya Mandir, 
Bhadreshwar (AVMB) 
Established in June 2012, 
AVMB is the second of four 
free schools operated by the 
Adani Foundation, serving 
children from socio-economically 
disadvantaged backgrounds, 
especially the fisherfolk 
community. Many students are 
first-generation learners, making 
the school a critical enabler of 
education in the region.
Adani Vidya Mandir, Krishnapatnam (AVMK)
Located in the Muthukur village, AVMK is an English-medium school offering free education from playschool to 
Class 10, along with books, uniforms, stationery, and midday meals, aligned with the state government curriculum.  Students enrolled in AVMB across 8

Impact CreatedAdani DAV Public School,

Established in April 2012 at 
Kuamara, Bhadrak, Adani DAV

Navchetan Vidyalaya Primary Wing (NVPW), Hazira, Surat
Located in Junagam, Hazira (Surat), NVPW is a Gujarati-medium primary school affiliated with the Gujarat 
State Education Board. Established in 2003 by Navchetan Vikas Mandal and currently managed by the Adani 
Foundation, the school focusses on activity-based learning to enhance engagement and academic outcomes.
Utthan:  
Nurturing Young Learners 
Programme Goal
To improve foundational literacy and 
numeracy in government primary 
schools while empowering learners 
from marginalised communitiesProgramme Description
Aligned with the National 
Education Policy (NEP) 2020, 
the Adani Foundation’s Utthan 
project focusses on enhancing 
learning capabilities in government 
primary schools through targeted 
interventions. The programme 
empowers Priya Vidyarthis 
(progressive learners) from 
marginalised backgrounds, catering 
to their specific learning needs. Each school is supported by an 
Utthan Sahayak, a dedicated 
teacher who plays a pivotal role 
in strengthening classroom 
practices and transforming 
schools into aspirational learning 
centres. The initiative makes 
learning engaging, provides 
essential resources and enhances 
teachers’ skills.
Extending its impact beyond regular 
school hours, Utthan also operates 
Adani Evening Education Centres 
(AEECs) to support students from 
underprivileged fishing and farming 
communities. These centres 
aim to reduce dropout rates, 
strengthen self-confidence, and 
improve academic outcomes at the 
secondary level. Each centre has a 
dedicated tutor and subject matter 
expert for every five students, 
focussing on Mathematics, 
English, and Science.Students

Beyond Boundaries:  
Sakina’s Story of Hope
Residing in the coastal village of Bhadreshwar, 
Sakina’s life revolved around the sea. Her family 
depended on fishing for survival, and while her 
parents encouraged her dreams, limited means 
could not transform her aspirations into reality. 
The turning point came when Sakina enrolled 
at Adani Vidya Mandir, Bhadreshwar, a school 
dedicated to nurturing potential. Her teachers 
saw immense resilience and dedication in Sakina. 
Later, her father met with a serious accident 
and was left bedridden. Sakina, the eldest 
child, shouldered new responsibilities. 
Education became more than an ambition; it became the key to a better future for her family. 
She excelled academically and embraced every 
opportunity - sports, music, and computer skills. 
She passed her Class 10 examinations with 
flying colours. 
Her journey did not stop there. With continued 
support from the Adani Foundation and Adani 
Vidya Mandir, Sakina secured admission to 
Tolani Polytechnic College, Adipur, pursuing 
engineering and becoming the first girl from her 
village to step outside its boundaries for higher 
education. She remains grateful to the Adani 
Foundation and Adani Vidya Mandir for turning 
her aspirations into achievements with constant 
support and guidance.STORY OF CHANGE

Organization (WHO), visual

or treatable. Nearly 90% of 
those affected reside in the low-

remains out of reach.

of vision problems. Eyeglasses are

Pathway to Dignity, Security 
and Independence
The Mangal Seva initiative by 
Adani Foundation is a targeted 
social welfare program designed 
to promote dignity, financial 
independence, and long-term 
security for newly married women 
with disabilities. Under this model, 
each selected beneficiary is 
supported through the creation 
of a fixed deposit of ⁠10 lakh for 
a period of 10 years. While the 
principal amount remains with 
them and is released at maturity, 
while a steady monthly interest payout (approximately ⁠5,416) 
provides regular income, enabling 
beneficiaries to meet household 
needs, investment towards 
livelihoods, access to healthcare, or 
pursuance of higher education.
The program adopts a structured, 
transparent selection and 
verification process involving field 
outreach, document validation, and 
home visits, ensuring that support 
reaches deserving candidates. 
Beyond financial assistance, Mangal 
Seva aims to strengthen social 
security and inclusion by enhancing 
the economic agency of women 
with disabilities and reducing their vulnerability post marriage. 
By combining financial planning 
with social empowerment, the 
initiative creates a sustainable 
pathway for improving quality 
of life and fostering long-term 
resilience among beneficiaries.
So far, the project has 
enrolled 500 beneficiaries and 
envisages to reach to 2000 
candidates over next four years. 
It is a collaborative program 
with multiple group companies 
participating in it.

Transforming Livelihoods Through Climate‑
Resilient Practices
In Lavachha village, Hazira, Shashikalaben 
Kishorbhai Patel, a 47-year-old widow and mother 
of two, struggled to sustain her family through 
farming. High irrigation costs and unreliable 
water supply forced her to cultivate only half 
of her 4 bighas of land, while dependence 
on diesel pumps drained her income and 
limited crop choices.
Her fate transformed with the launch of the 
Adani Foundation’s Solar Pump Initiative, which 
introduced a clean, affordable, and sustainable 
irrigation solution. Shashikalaben embraced 
the opportunity and began cultivating her 
entire landholding, diversified into crops 
such as jowar, wheat, bajra, tuver, chawli, and 
ladyfinger, and significantly reduced operating costs. Stable incomes enabled savings and 
reinvestment, while improving productivity 
and strengthening her financial independence. 
Improved financial stability led to better 
education for her children, enhanced quality of 
life, and growing confidence, positioning her as a 
role model for women in the village.
Shashikalaben’s success sparked a ripple 
effect, encouraging other farmers to adopt 
solar-powered irrigation, reduce reliance on fossil 
fuels, and shift towards environment-friendly, 
climate-resilient farming practices. Today, the 
initiative has enabled over 100 farmers in 
Lavachha and nearby villages to lower irrigation 
costs, improve yields, and shift to sustainable 
agriculture, enhancing rural incomes 
and livelihoods.STORY OF CHANGE

Fulfilling Aspirations with Adani Coaching & 
Fitness Centre
At the Adani Coaching & Fitness Centre in 
Gangavaram, Andhra Pradesh, sports have 
become a powerful platform for transformation. 
Established in 2024, the centre offers structured 
coaching in Kabaddi, Kho-Kho, Shuttle Badminton, 
along with fitness training for youth aspiring to join 
the Armed Forces and Police, opening doors for 
underprivileged communities.
Among the many inspiring journeys are those of 
Yeripalli Komali (16), Badi Divya (16), and Perla Divya 
(20), three young athletes preparing to represent 
Gangavaram/Andhra Pradesh at a national-level 
Kabaddi championship. Komali, a first-generation 
learner from a fisherfolk family, balances school with daily practice and has already competed in 
multiple national tournaments. Divya’s journey from 
zonal competitions to the national stage reflects grit 
and determination amid economic hardships. Perla, a 
two-time All-India Kabaddi participant, works as a 
Physical Education teacher and earns a steady income.
The centre provides holistic support through rigorous 
selection process, professional coaching, mentorship, 
sports kits, and structured fitness programmes for 
career aspirants. Around 72 athletes, including 30 
girls, have been trained here; four players have already 
represented Gangavaram at national tournaments, with 
participants reporting improved confidence and fitness.
Central to this transformation is Nolli Theja (23), a 
national-level Kabaddi player with 14 championships, 
who overcame significant hardships to become a 
role model for the next generation. Together, these 
stories reaffirm the Adani Foundation’s commitment 
to nurturing talent, breaking barriers, and creating 
opportunities for youth in rural India.STORY OF CHANGE

mandatory to foster a culture of sustainable procurement backed by mutual respect.

Strengthening Supply Chain with Supplier ESG Programme
The Supplier ESG Programme at APSEZ is aimed at strengthening our supply across operations. It helps drive 
efficiency and sustainability through a series of initiatives that enable easy identification and assessment of 
potential ESG risks, while empowering us to effectively address such risks. It further empowers us to easily track 
supplier performance and take prompt, necessary corrective actions.
Programme Interventions
SUPPLIER ESG PROGRAMMEMinimum ESG Requirements and Exclusion of Non‑Compliant Suppliers: 
It is mandatory for our suppliers to meet specific minimum ESG 
requirements, and deviation leads to their exclusion.
Preferring Suppliers with Enhanced ESG Profiles: The company prefers 
suppliers demonstrating excellence in ESG practices. Selection and 
contracting of contractors involves assigning of significant weightage 
to ESG criteria. This underlines our commitment to recognising and 
rewarding those who contribute positively to environmental protection, 
social well-being, and excellence in governance. It further helps 
incentivise superior ESG performance while aligning with our broader 
sustainability goals.
Training Buyers and Internal Stakeholders: Contractors are extensively 
trained on social aspects of ESG, including fair labour practices and 
ethical procurement.
Oversight of Supplier ESG Programme: The ESG Programme is overseen 
by the Board Corporate Responsibility Committee. This helps ensure 
integration of the programme into the corporate strategy and resource 
allocation methodology. This Committee reports directly to the Board on 
the programme status and progress.
Periodic Evaluation of Purchasing Practices: Alignment of procurement 
activities with our Supplier Code of Conduct and ESG standards is 
ensured through periodic evaluation. The process involves scrutiny of the 
suppliers' compliance with our established ESG metrics, underlining our 
commitment to sustainability and ethical practices.SOCIAL
We have consciously adopted a well-defined diligent supplier screening process to address the complexities and 
potential risks inherent in our supply chain. The process is aligned to our insights into the global environmental, 
social, financial, and business relevance risks and challenges. It enables identification of critical suppliers, aiding 
us in effective risk monitoring and management with respect to suppliers with the highest potential impact. 
This translates into enhanced resilience and sustainability of our supply chain.Well‑structured Supplier Ecosystem
We follow well-defined vendor registration and onboarding 
processes to strengthen the reliability and efficiency of our 
supplier ecosystem while ensuring compliance with the highest 
ethical standards and operational conduct. Besides helping to 
mitigate risks associated with third-party engagements, these 
processes support in reducing the potential financial liabilities 
and protecting the company’s reputation.

Contractor Safety Management and

Our supplier screening framework prioritises partners who are critical 
of operations and difficult to substitute due to the uniqueness or 
strategic importance of their offerings. High-volume suppliers and 
essential component providers are digitally mapped within Project 
SETU, enabling centralised monitoring, enhanced risk visibility, and 
proactive risk management.To enable this project, we have formulated a digital platform for our desk-based assessment for our 
suppliers in collaboration with our partner. This platform will serve as a single window for:
 �Uploading ESG performance data and supporting documents
 �Managing compliance reporting under BRSR Core and other frameworks like GRI, CDP, etc
 �Enabling training, awareness sessions, and regular updates
 �Ensuring confidentiality, traceability, and verification of information
Supplier evaluations under Project SETU include a comprehensive 
review of ESG performance, covering historical commitments and 
ongoing actions to mitigate environmental, social, and governance 
risks. The process also incorporates contextual factors such as 
geographical, sectoral, and commodity-specific vulnerabilities, 
ensuring a nuanced and forward-looking assessment.
To ensure objectivity, APSEZ has implemented a Sustainability 
Risk Matrix that classifies suppliers based on ESG parameters and 
assigns overall grades. This matrix identifies suppliers with elevated 
sustainability risks as well as those demonstrating leadership in ESG 
practices. Project SETU digitises this methodology, offering real-time 
analytics, risk flags, and performance comparisons to support 
responsible sourcing decisions.
Project SETU is designed to engage suppliers, customers, and partners 
in a recurring assessment exercise that:
 �Collects reliable ESG performance data across the value chain

resource efficiency
 �Promotes health, safety, labour rights, diversity, equity, and inclusion

10% assigned for safety and compliance, and the rest for overall performance. Suppliers are mandated to maintain 
a minimum score of 90, updated monthly.

RFID mesh
Implementation of RFID mesh technology has helped 
establish a wireless network for connecting sensor devices.
We have successfully piloted the tracking of high-value 
containers in real-time, monitoring and detection of air 
pollution, automatic energy management and vehicle 
movement control, among other applications.
3D Scanning Technique
3D mapping technique was explored to obtain real-time 
profiles of bulk piles in the stock yard, for use in effective 
yard planning. This enabled us to measure the area occupied/
available for cargo weight at any given point
Algorithmic Optimisation
Algorithmic optimisation was tested to create dynamic 
vessel plans, which were then implemented through a central 
control room for optimal utilisation of port equipment.
Video Analytics

Identify the need for a PIA Determine if the project involves high-risk data processing activities, 
such as handling sensitive personal information
Describe the Information Flows Document the process of collection, usage, storage, and sharing of the 
collected
Identify Privacy Risks Assess potential risks to individuals' privacy, including data breaches or 
misuse
Consult Stakeholders Engage with stakeholders, including data subjects, to gather their input 
and concerns
Evaluate Privacy Solutions Identify measures to mitigate identified risks, such as data encryption or 
access controls
Document the PIA Record the findings and decisions made during the assessment
Review and Update Regularly review and update the PIA to reflect changes in the project or 
regulatory environment

Independent Assurance Statement  
To, 
Adani Ports & Special Economic Zone Ltd. (APSEZL),  
Adani Corporate House, Shantigram,  
Near Vaishno Devi Circle, S. G. Highway, Khodiyar  
Ahmedabad -382421, Gujarat, India  
Adani Ports & Special Economic Zone Limited (hereinafter referred to as "APSEZL" or the "Reporting Organization") engaged TUV  India 
Private Limited ("TUVI") to perform an independent external assurance of the non -financial disclosures reported in APSEZL's 
Sustainability Report (hereinafter the "Report") prepared with reference to the principles of GRI Standards 2021 (hereafter " GRI") and 
the IIRC Integrated Reporting (<IR>) Framework. The Report covers APSEZL's ESG performance for the period 01/04/2025 to 
31/03/2026 , and the verification was conducted within the reporting boundary between 08/12/2025 and 18/03/2026 . 
This assurance engagement was conducted in accordance with the AA1000 Assurance Standard v3 — Type 2, Moderate Level  and 
ISAE 3000 (Revised) — Reasonable Level. TUVI confirms that, prior to acceptance of the engagement, the preconditions for the 
assurance engagement were assessed in accordance with ISAE 3000 (Revised). TUVI determined that the subject matter is support ed 
by suitable criteria (GRI Standards 2021 and the <IR> Framework), management has acknowledged its responsibility for the preparation 
and presentation of the sustainability information and for providing  access to relevant records, and that sufficient appropriate evidence 
was expected to be available to support the assurance conclusion. Accordingly, the engagement was accepted and performed in 
accordance with ISAE 3000 (Revised) and AA1000AS v3. These two  standards govern distinct assurance tracks with separately defined 
scopes, procedures, and conclusions: ISAE 3000 (Revised) applies to the reasonable assurance engagement over GRI Standards 20 21 
and IIRC <IR> Framework disclosures, while AA1000AS v3 appli es to the Type 2 Moderate Level assurance over adherence to the 
AA1000 AccountAbility Principles. The procedures applied and conclusions expressed under each standard are presented separate ly 
within this statement.  
The assurance process was conducted with reference to the following applicable frameworks and guidelines:  
• GRI Standards 2021, including GRI 1: Foundation, GRI 2: General Disclosures, GRI 3: Material Topics, and applicable Topic -
specific Standards (300 and 400 series);  
• IIRC Integrated Reporting Framework (<IR>); and  
• AA1000 AccountAbility Principles Standard (AA1000 AP 2018) and AA1000 Assurance Standard v3 (AA1000AS v3).  
Management's Responsibility  
APSEZL has developed the Report content and is responsible for identifying material topics through its materiality determinat ion 
process, determining the corresponding ESG issues, and establishing processes for performance management, data management, an d 
data quality.  
APSEZL is responsible for the Report content relating to the GRI Standards 2021 disclosures and the six -capitals disclosures aligned with 
the <IR> Framework. Its management is accountable for the collection, analysis, preparation, and disclosure of the inf ormation 
presented in the Report, whether in web -based or printed format.  
APSEZL's management ensures that the Report is prepared accurately with reference to the applied criteria — the GRI Standards 2021 
and the <IR> Framework — and is free from material misstatements. This responsibility includes maintaining the integrity of t he 
company's website, complying with applicable laws, archiving and reproducing disclosed information, and making such data avai lable 
to relevant stakeholders upon request.  
Any partial reproduction of this assurance statement may lead to misinterpretation of its scope, procedures, and conclusions.  
Therefore, the assurance conclusion should be read in its entirety, together with the defined scope, methodology, limitations , and  
criteria described in this statement.

Assurance Methodology  
TUVI adopted a risk -based approach, focusing verification efforts on disclosures and issues of high material relevance to APSEZL and 
its stakeholders. The objective was to assess the reliability and accuracy of the non -financial information disclosed, with  emphasis on 
the robustness of data management systems, internal controls, and information flows. TUVI's assurance activities included:  
1. Document and Data Review  
• Examination of documents, datasets, and supporting evidence provided by APSEZL, covering the management approach and 
performance disclosures for all material GRI Topic -specific Standards and <IR> capital -related disclosures;  
• Evaluation of disclosure quality, clarity, and completeness against the requirements of the GRI Standards 2021 and the <IR> 
Framework; and  
• Review of APSEZL's approach to stakeholder engagement and the materiality determination process.  
2. Stakeholder Interviews  
• Conducted interviews with key representatives, including data owners, process managers, and decision -makers across various 
departments and port operations of APSEZL, through onsite visits and remote assessments; and  
• Reviewed qualitative statements included in the Report to assess their consistency with responses received during interviews 
and the evidence reviewed.  
3. Process and System Assessment  
• Review of systems and processes for implementing ESG and sustainability -related policies as described in the Report; and  
• Assessment of data management systems and internal processes supporting the preparation of ESG disclosures, including data 
flows, aggregation procedures, and supporting records.  
4. Substantive Testing  
TUVI performed walkthrough procedures to understand ESG data flows and substantive testing including document verification, 
recalculation, analytical review, and data traceability checks for selected KPIs and disclosures. Examples of KPI -category procedure s 
applied:  
• GHG Emissions  — Recalculation of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions and related emission intensity using primary fuel and electricity 
consumption data; verification of Scope 1 sources such as diesel, natural gas and furnace oil used in equipment and vehicles,  
Scope 2 electr icity consumption, and application of GHG Protocol methodology and emission factors; For each reported Scope 3 
category, TUVI verified the data quality hierarchy by tracing activity inputs — such as procurement records, fuel purchase 
invoices, logistics co ntracts, travel booking systems, and asset registers — against the emission factors and calculation methods 
applied, confirming alignment with the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard. Where primary supplier data 
was unavailable, TUVI asse ssed the appropriateness of secondary or proxy factors by cross -referencing against recognized 
databases including IPCC, IEA, and GHG Protocol Technical Guidance sector coefficients through document review and 
management interviews. Verification procedures  also included consistency checks of category -level totals against prior -year 
figures, internal aggregation workpapers, and the organization’s GHG inventory tool, with findings retained in TUVI's engagem ent 
workpapers . 
• Energy  — Verification of total energy consumption from renewable and non -renewable sources, including renewable electricity, 
non-renewable electricity and fuel consumption; cross -verification of meter readings, utility bills, fuel invoices and renewable 
generati on records, including captive solar and wind power data; validation of energy intensity calculations.  
• Water  — Verification of water withdrawal and consumption by source, including surface water, groundwater, third -party water, 
seawater/desalinated water and other sources; traceability to municipal/third -party supply records, groundwater permissions,  
www.tuv -nord.com/in  
TÜV® 
 
 
desalination/source records and site -level water logs; review of water discharge, zero liquid discharge compliance, treated water 
reuse and recycling records.  
• Safety  — Verification of employee and contractor safety KPIs, including Lost Time Injury, Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate, 
fatalities and total person -hours worked, against site -level incident registers, investigation records, HR/attendance records, 
contractor w orkforce records, corrective action evidence and APSEZ safety management system requirements.  
• Waste  — Reconciliation of waste generated, recovered and disposed by category, including plastic waste, e -waste, biomedical 
waste, construction and demolition waste, battery waste, hazardous waste and non -hazardous waste; verification of recycling, 
reuse, recov ery and disposal records against CPCB/SPCB registered CHWIF/TSDF records, authorised recycler certificates, disposal 
manifests, Zero Waste to Landfill records and site -level waste registers.  
5. Sampling Methodology  
TUVI applied a risk -based sampling methodology to select representative samples of ESG disclosures, considering materiality, risk of 
misstatement, data complexity, estimation uncertainty, nature and scale of operations, geographical spread of port and logi stics 
facilities, and site contribution to ESG impacts. Sample selection prioritised locations with significant operational impact and KPIs with 
higher inherent risk.  
Site Verification Coverage:  Onsite verification was conducted at 6 of 15 domestic ports/terminals (Dhamra, Gangavaram, 
Krishnapatnam, Vizhinjam, Hazira, and Mundra), along with the Corporate Office, Ahmedabad  complemented by a complete desk 
review of GRI disclosure data across all remaining ports, terminals, logistics parks, and offices within the reporting bounda ry. TUVI 
applied a stratified, risk -based sampling methodology for onsite verification to support the reasonable assurance conclusion across 
APSEZL’s reporting boundary, considering operational significance, ESG risk, operational/geographical diversity, bounda ry changes, 
emerging exposures, and centrally administered functions. Workforce and HR KPIs, in cluding safety, training, diversity and 
employment, were fully covered as these are centrally managed and reported by the Corporate Office. For remaining domestic po rts, 
terminals, logistics parks, agri silos, warehouses and international operations, TUVI performed substantive desk review procedures 
covering source records, reconciliations, analytical reviews, remote walkthroughs, targeted clarifications, and consolidation /QA-QC 
controls. This combined onsite and desk -review approach, supported by APSEZL’s standardised ESG data framework, common KPI 
methodologies, centralised QA/QC review and homogeneous process controls, provided sufficient appropriate evidence to support  the 
reasonable assurance conclusion in accordance with  agreed scope of work . 
KPI-Specific Materiality Approach:  A KPI -specific materiality approach was applied: (i) a 5% quantitative threshold  was applied to 
volume -based KPIs (GHG emissions, energy, water, waste, and wages); and (ii) a qualitative zero -tolerance threshold  was applied to 
high -risk ESG indicators — fatalities, permanent disabilities, POSH complaints upheld, regulatory non -compliances, and customer data 
breaches  — for which any occurrence is treated as material irrespective of magnitude. Where disclosures are based on estimation or 
standard assumptions (e.g., energy consumption for leased offices estimated using headcount -based methodologies, vehicular fuel 
estimated from distance and fuel -efficiency assumptions), the estimation uncertainty has been acknowledged and factored into the 
assurance conclusion. APSEZL is encouraged to supplement estimated KPIs with explicit quantitative uncertainty ranges or sens itivity 
analysis in future reporting p eriods to further enhance the reliability and comparability of estimated disclosures. The reasonable 
assurance conclusion applies to the selected GRI disclosures listed in the scope table above, and not to all GRI disclosures in the Report; 
the risk -based sampling approach is designed to provide a sufficient evidential basis for the conclusions expressed on the listed 
disclosures.  
The Report was evaluated against the following criteria: stakeholder inclusiveness, materiality, responsiveness, completeness, 
neutrality, relevance, sustainability context, accuracy, reliability, comparability, clarity, and timeliness , as prescribed in the GRI 
Standards 2021, the <IR> Framework, and AA1000AS v3 along with AA1000 AP (2018).

A. ISAE 3000 (Revised) — Reasonable Assurance Conclusion:  Based on the procedures performed and evidence obtained, in our 
opinion, the selected ESG disclosures presented in APSEZL's Sustainability Report for the period 01/04/2025 to 31/03/2026 hav e been 
prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable reporting criteria of the GRI Standards 2021 and the <IR> 
Framework, and fairly represent APSEZL's sustainability performance within the defined scope without material misstatement.  
B. AA1000AS v3 — Type 2 Moderate Assurance Conclusion:  Based on the procedures performed and evidence obtained, in our 
opinion, APSEZL has adhered, in all material respects, to the AA1000 AccountAbility Principles of Inclusivity, Materiality, 
Responsiveness, and Impact . The selected performance information subject to the moderate assurance engagement is reliable in all 
material respects.  
TUVI confirms that APSEZL has transparently reported major material information pertaining to all its six capitals in line wi th the 
<IR> framework, as below:  
Financial Capital:  APSEZL creates value and drives growth by optimal utilization of funds raised from various providers of capital.  
Manufactured Capital:  APSEZL operates an integrated logistics network equipped with modern technology and infrastructure, enabling 
stable and scalable operations diversified across geographies.  
Intellectual Capital:  APSEZL leverages a robust technology infrastructure that drives operational efficiency and customer satisfaction, 
including efficient transport utility with pricing power, real -time vessel tracking services, and knowledge -based intangibles such as 
intellectual property and process know -how.  
Human Capital:  APSEZL focuses on attracting, developing, and retaining talent by providing training and ensuring overall safety and 
well-being, while promoting inclusion and diversity throughout the business.  
Social and Relationship Capital:  APSEZL maintains relationships with stakeholders such as customers, business partners, regulators, 
suppliers, communities, legislators, and policy -makers, and creates value beyond its boundaries by cultivating an ethos of giving back 
to society through CS R initiatives and building a sustainable, resilient value chain.  
Natural Capital:  APSEZL emphasizes operational eco -efficiency, principles of circularity and resource efficiency, and product 
stewardship standards for being environmentally responsible throughout its value chain — covering responsible sourcing, emissions, 
water consumption, and waste management.  
Evaluation of Adherence to AA1000 AccountAbility Principles and Other Contemporary Principles  
Stakeholder Inclusiveness:  Stakeholder identification and engagement is carried out by APSEZL on a periodic basis to bring out key 
stakeholder concerns as material topics of significant stakeholders. In our view, the Report meets the requirements.  
Sustainability Context:  APSEZL has established the relationship between ESG and organizational strategy within the Report, as well as 
the context in which disclosures are made. In our view, the Report meets the requirements with regard to sustainability conte xt. 
Materiality:  The materiality determination process has been conducted based on the requirements of the GRI Standards 2021 and 
AA1000 AP, considering the involvement of internal and external stakeholders across the upstream and downstream value chain. The 
Report fairly  brings out the aspects, topics, and their respective boundaries across the diverse operations of APSEZL. In our view, the 
Report meets the requirements.  
Responsiveness:  TUVI believes that the responses to the material aspects identified through the materiality determination process are 
fairly articulated in the Report, including disclosures on APSEZL's policies, management systems, and governance. In our view , the 
Report  meets the requirements.
